# On Minimum Generalized Manhattan Connections **Abstract** We consider minimum-cardinality Manhattan connected sets with arbitrary demands: Given a collection of points _P_ in the plane, together with a subset of pairs of points in _P_ (which we call _demands_), find a minimum-cardinality superset of _P_ such that every demand pair is connected by a path whose length is the \(\ell_1\)-distance of the pair. This problem is a variant of three well- studied problems that have arisen in computational geometry, data structures, and network design: (i) It is a node-cost variant of the classical Manhattan network problem, (ii) it is an extension of the binary search tree problem to arbitrary demands, and (iii) it is a special case of the directed Steiner forest problem. Since the problem inherits basic structural properties from the context of binary search trees, an _O_(log_n_)-approximation is trivial. We show that the problem is NP-hard and present an \(O(\sqrt{logn})\)-approximation algorithm. Moreover, we provide an _O_(loglog_n_)-approximation algorithm for complete _k_-partite demands as well as improved results for unit-disk demands and several generalizations. Our results crucially rely on a new lower bound on the optimal cost that could potentially be useful in the context of BSTs. ### 1 Introduction Given a collection of points \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\) on the plane, the _Manhattan Graph GP_ of _P_ is an undirected graph with vertex set _V(GP_)=_P_ and arcs _E(GP_) that connect any vertically- or horizontally- aligned points. Point _p_ is said to be _Manhattan-connected (M-connected)_ to point _q_ if _GP_ contains a shortest rectilinear path from _p_ to _q_ (i.e. a path of length ||_p-q_||1). In this paper, we initiate the study of the following problem: Given points \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\) and demands \(D\subseteq P\times P\), we want to find a smallest set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\) such that every pair of vertices in _D_ is _M_-connected in \(G_{P\cup Q}\). We call this problem Minimum Generalized Manhattan Connections (MinGMConn), see Figure 1 for an illustration. **Binary Search Trees (BSTs).**

The _Dynamic Optimality Conjecture_ \[18\] is one of the most fundamental open problems in dynamic data structures, postulating the existence of an _O_(1)- competitive binary search tree. Despite continuing efforts and important progress for several decades (see, e.g., \[10, 6, 9, 17, 2\] and references therein), the conjecture has so far remained elusive, with the best known competitive ratio of _O_(loglog_n_) obtained by Tango trees \[10\]. Even in the offline setting, the best known algorithm is also a _O_(loglog_n_)-approximation; the problem is not even known to be NP-hard. Demaine, Harmon, Iacono, Kane, and Pătraşcu \[9\] showed that approximating BST is equivalent (up to a constant in the approximation factor) to approximating the node-cost Manhattan problem with "evolving demand" (that is, points added to the solution create demands to all existing points).<sup>1</sup>

The long-standing nature of the _O_(loglog_n_) upper bound could suggest the lower bound answer. However, the understanding of lower bound techniques for BSTs has been completely lacking: It is not even known whether the problem is NP-hard! Our work is inspired by the following question.

Is it NP-hard to (exactly) compute a minimum cost binary search tree?

We are, unfortunately, unable to answer this question. In this paper, we instead present a proof that a natural generalization of the problem in the geometric view (which is exactly our MinGMConn) is NP-hard<sup>2</sup>. We believe that our construction and its analysis could be useful in further study of the BST problem from the perspective of lower bounds.

**Edge-Cost Manhattan Problem.**

Closely related to MinGMConn is the edge-cost variant of Manhattan Network \[14\]: Given \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\), our goal is to compute \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\) such that every pair in _P_ is _M_-connected in \(G_{P\cup Q}\), while minimizing the total lengths of the edges used for the connections. The problem is motivated by various applications in city planning, network layouts, distributed algorithms and VLSI circuit design, and has received attention in the computational geometry community. Since the edge-cost variant is NP-hard \[5\], the focus has been on approximation algorithms. Several groups of researchers presented 2-approximation algorithms \[15, 4\], and this has remained the best known approximation ratio. Generalizations of the edge-cost variant have been proposed<tbc>

**Directed Steiner Forests (DSF).** MinGMConn is a special case of _node-cost directed Steiner forest (DSF):_ Given a directed graph _G_=(_V,E_) and pairs of terminals \(\mathcal{D}\subseteq V\times V\) , find a minimum cardinality subset \(S\subseteq V\) such that _G_\[_S_\] contains a path from _s_ to _t_ for all \((s,t)\in\mathcal{D}\). DSF is known to be highly intractable, with hardness \(2^{log^{1-\epsilon}|V|}\) unless \(\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{DTIME}(n^{polylogn})\) \[11\]. The best known approximation ratios are slightly sub-linear \[3, 12\]. Manhattan problems can be thought of as natural, tractable special cases of DSF, with approximability between constant and logarithmic regimes. For more details, see \[8\].

## 1.1 Our Contributions

In this paper, we present both hardness and algorithmic results for MinGMConn.

**Theorem 1.** _The_ MinGMConn _problem is NP-hard, even for an input that contains at most one point per row and column._

This result can be thought of as a first step towards developing structural understanding of Manhattan connectivity with respect to lower bounds. We believe that such an understanding would come in handy in future study of binary search trees in the geometric view.

Next, we present algorithmic results. Due to the BST structures, an _O_(log_n_)-approximation is trivial. The main ingredient in obtaining a sub-logarithmic approximation is an approximation algorithm for the case of "few" _x_-coordinates. More formally, we say that an input instance is _s-thin_ if the points in _P_ lie on at most _s_ different _x_-coordinates.

**Theorem 2.** _There exists an efficient O_(log_s)-approximation algorithm for an s-thin instance_ (_P,D_) _of_ MinGMConn.

In fact, our algorithm produces solutions with \(O(logs\cdot\mathsf{IS}(P,D))\) many points, where \(\mathsf{IS}(P,D)\le\mathsf{OPT}(P,D)\) is the cardinality of a _boundary independent set_ (a notion introduced below). This theorem is tight up to a constant factor, since there exists an input instance (_P,D_) on _s_ different columns such that the \(\mathsf{OPT}(P,D)=\Omega(\mathsf{IS}(P,D)logs)\); see Appendix C.

This theorem, along with the boundary independent set analysis, turns out to be an important building block for our approximation result, which achieves an approximation ratio that is sublogarithmic in _n_.

**Theorem 3.** _There is an efficient_ \(O(\sqrt{logn})\)_-approximation algorithm for_ MinGMConn.

This gives an improvement over the trivial _O_(log_n_)-approximation and may grant some new hope with regards to improving the _O_(log_n_)-approximation for the edge-cost variants.

We provide improved approximation ratios for settings when the graph formed by the demands has a special structure.

**Theorem 4.** _There is an O_(loglog_n)-approximation algorithm for_ MinGMConn _when the demands form a complete k-partite graph._

Another set of such results concerns settings where the demand graph is derived from geometry. Here, points _p,q_ form a demand if they are within a certain distance _r_ (possibly dependent on _p_ and _q_) of each other.

**Theorem 5.** _For unit-disk demands,_ MinGMConn _admits an O_(1)_-approximation. For two-disk demands, we can achieve an O_(loglog_n)-approximation. For (general) disk demands with maximal radius ratio_ \(\Delta\)_, there is an_ \(O(log\Delta)\)_-approximation._

## 1.2 Overview of Techniques

The NP-hardness proof is based on a reduction to 3-SAT. In contrast to the uniform case of MinGMConn, the non-uniform case allows us to encode the structure of a 3-SAT formula in a geometrical manner: we can use demand rectangles to form certain "paths" (see Figure 2). We exploit this observation in the reduction design by translating clauses and variables into _gadgets_, rectangular areas with specific placement of input points and demands (see Figure 3). Variable gadgets are placed between clause gadgets and a dedicated _starting point_. The crux is to design the instance such that a natural solution to the intra- and inter-gadget demands connects the starting point to either the positive or the negative part of each variable gadget. And, the M-paths leaving a variable gadget from that part can all reach _only_ clauses with a _positive_ appearance or _only_ clauses with a _negative_ appearance of that variable respectively. We refer to such solutions as _boolean solutions_, as they naturally correspond to a variable assignment. Additional demands between the starting point and the clause gadgets are satisfied by a boolean solution if and only if it corresponds to a satisfying variable assignment. The main part of the proof is to show that any small-enough solution is a boolean solution.

In the study of any optimization (in particular, minimization) problem, one of the main difficulties is to come up with a strong lower bound on the cost of an optimal solution that can be leveraged by algorithms. For binary search trees, many such bounds were known, and the strongest known lower bound is called an _independent rectangle bound (IR)_. However, IR is provably too weak for the purpose of MinGMConn, that is, the gap between the optimal and IR can be as large as \(\Omega(n)\). We propose to use a new bound, which we call _vertically separable demands (VS)_. This bound turns out to be relatively tight and plays an important role in both our hardness and algorithmic results. In the hardness result, we use our VS bound to argue about the cost of the optimal in the soundness case.

Our \(O(\sqrt{logn})\)-approximation follows the high-level idea of \[1\], which presents a geometric _O_(loglog_n_)-approximation for BST. Roughly speaking, it argues (implicitly) that two combinatorial properties, which we refer to as (A) and (B), are sufficient for the existence of an _O_(loglog_n_)- approximation: (A) the lower bound function is "subadditive" with respect to a certain instance partitioning, and (B) the instance is "sparse" in the sense that for any input (_P,D_), there exists an equivalent input \((P',D')\) such that \(|P'|=O(\mathsf{OPT}(P,D))\). In the context of BST, (A) holds for the Wilber bound and (B) is almost trivial to show.

In the MinGMConn problem, we prove that Property (A) holds for the new VS bound. However, proving Property (B) seems to be very challenging. We instead show a corollary of Property (B): There is an _O_(log_s_)-approximation algorithm for MinGMConn, where _s_ is the number of columns containing at least one input point. The proof of this relaxed property is the main new ingredient of our algorithmic result and is stated in Theorem 2. Finally, we argue that this weaker property still suffices for an \(O(\sqrt{logn})\)-approximation algorithm. For completeness, in Sections F and G, we discuss special cases (see Theorems 4 and 5) where we prove that Property (B) holds and thus an _O_(loglog_n_)-approximation exists.

### 1.3 Outlook and Open Problems

Inspired by the study of structural properties of Manhattan connected sets and potential applications in BSTs, we initiate the study of MinGMConn by proving NP-hardness and giving several algorithmic results.

There are multiple interesting open problems. First, can we show that the BST problem is NP-hard? We hope that our construction and analysis using the new VS bound would be useful for this purpose. Another interesting open problem is to obtain a _o_(log_n_)-approximation for the edge-cost variant of the generalized Manhattan network problem.

Finally, it can be shown that our VS bound is sandwiched between OPT and IR. It is an interesting question to study the tightness of the VS bound when estimating the value of an optimal solution. Can we show that VS is within a constant factor from the optimal cost of BST? Can we approximate the value of VS efficiently within a constant factor?

## 2 Model & Preliminaries

Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\) be a set of points on the plane. We say that points \(p,q\in P\) are _Manhattan-connected (M-connected)_ in _P_ if there is a sequence of points _p=x_<sub>0</sub>_,x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>k</sub>=q_ such that (i) the points _x<sub>i</sub>_ and _x_<sub>_i_+1</sub> are horizontally or vertically aligned for _i_=0_,...,k_-1, and (ii) the total length satis fies \(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}||x_i-x_{i+1}||_1=||p-q||_1\).

In the _minimum generalized Manhattan connections_ (MinGMConn) _problem_, we are given a set of _input points P_ and their placement in a rectangular grid with integer coordinates such that there are no two points in the same row or in the same column. Additionally, we are given a set \(D\subseteq\{(p,q)|p,q\in P\}\) of _demands_. The goal is to find a set of points _Q_ of minimum cardinality such that _p_ and _q_ are M-connected with respect to \(P\cup Q\) for all \((p,q)\in D\). Denote by OPT(_P,D_) the size of such a point set. We differentiate between the points of _P_ and _Q_ by calling them _input points_ and _auxiliary points_, respectively. Since being M-connected is a symmetrical relation, we typically assume _x(p)\<x(q_) for all \((p,q)\in D\). Here, _x(p_) and _y(p_) denote the _x_- and _y_-coordinate of a point _p_, respectively. In our analysis, we sometimes use the notations \[_n_\]:={1,2_,...,n_} and \([n]_0:=[n]\cup\{0\}\), where \(n\in\mathbb{N}\).

#### Connection to Binary Search Trees.

In the _uniform_ case where all pairs of input points are connected by a demand, i.e. \(D=\{(p,q)|p,q\in P\}\), this problem is intimately connected to the Binary Search Tree (BST) problem in the geometric model \[9\]. Here, we are given a point set _P_ and the goal is to compute a minimum set _Q_ such that _every pair_ in \(P\cup Q\) is M-connected in \(P\cup Q\). Denote by BST(_P_) the optimal value of the BST problem.

#### Independent Rectangles and Vertically Separable Demands.

Following Demaine et al. \[9\], we define the independent rectangle number which is a lower bound on OPT(_P,D_). For a demand \((p,q)\in D\), denote by _R(p,q_) the (unique) axis-aligned closed rectangle that has _p_ and _q_ as two of its corners. We call it the _demand rectangle_ corresponding to (_p,q_). Two rectangles \(R(p,q),R(p',q')\) are called _non-conflicting_ if none contains a corner of the other in its interior. We say a subset of demands \(D'\subseteq D\) is _independent_, if all pairs of rectangles in \(D'\) are non-conflicting. Denote by IR(_P,D_) the maximum integer _k_ such that there is an independent subset \(D'\) of size _k_. We refer to _k_ as the _independent rectangle number_.

For uniform demands, the problem admits a 2-approximation. Here, the independent rectangle number plays a crucial role. Specifically, it was argued in Harmon’s PhD thesis \[16\] that a natural greedy algorithm costs at most the independent rectangle number and thus yields a 2-approximation.<tbc>

In our generalized demand case, however, the independent rectangle number turns out to be a bad estimate on the value of an optimal solution. Instead, we consider the notion of vertically separable demands, used implicitly in \[9\].

We say that a subset of demands \(D'\subseteq D\) is _vertically separable_ if there exists an ordering _R_<sub>1</sub>_,R_<sub>2</sub>_,...,R<sub>k</sub>_ of its demand rectangles and vertical line segments \(\ell_1,\ell_2\dots,\ell_k\) such that \(\ell_i\) connects the respective interiors of top and bottom boundaries of _R<sub>i</sub>_ and does not intersect any _R<sub>j</sub>_, for _j\>i_. For an input (_P,D_), denote by V5(_P,D_) the maximum cardinality of such a subset. We call a set of demands _D monotone_, if either _y(p)\<y(q_) for all \((p,q)\in D\) or _y(p)\>y(q_) for all \((p,q)\in D\). We assume the former case holds as both are symmetrical. In the following, we argue that V5 is indeed a lower bound on OPT (proof in Appendix B).

**Lemma 6** (\[9\])**.** _Let_ (_P,D_) _be an input for_ MinGMConn_. If D is monotone, then we have_ \(\mathsf{IR}(P,D)\le\mathsf{V5}(P,D)\le\mathsf{OPT}(P,D)\)_. Thus, in general,_ \(\frac{1}{2}\mathsf{IR}(P,D)\le\mathsf{V5}(P,D)\le 2\cdot\mathsf{OPT}(P,D)\).

The charging scheme described in the proof of Lemma 6 injectively maps a demand rectangle _R_ to a point of the optimal solution that lies in _R_. This implies the following corollary.

**Corollary 7.** _Let D be a vertically separable, monotone set of demands and Q a feasible solution. If_ |_Q_|=|_D|, there is a bijection_ \(c:Q\rightarrow D\) _such that_ \(q\in R(c(q))\) _for all_ \(q\in Q\)_. In particular, for_ \(Q'\subseteq Q\) _there are at least_ \(|Q'|\) _demands from D that each covers some_ \(q\in Q'\).

In general, the independent rectangle number and the maximum size of a vertically separable set are incomparable. By Lemma 6, we have \(\mathsf{IR}(P,D)\le 2\cdot\mathsf{V5}(P,D)\). However, IR(_P,D_) may be smaller than V5(_P,D_) up to a factor of _n_. To see this, consider _n_ diagonally shifted copies of a demand, e.g. _R<sub>i</sub>=R_\(\big(\)(_i,i),(i+n,i+n_)\(\big)\), for _i_=1_,...,n_. Here, IR(_P,D_)=1 and V5(_P,D_)=_n_. Thus, the concept of vertical separability is more useful as a lower bound.

## 3 NP-hardness

In this section, we show Theorem 1 by reducing the MinGMConn problem to 3-SAT. In 3-SAT, we are given a formula \(\phi\) consisting of _m_ clauses _C_<sub>1</sub>_,C_<sub>2</sub>_,...,C<sub>m</sub>_ over _n_ variables _X_<sub>1</sub>_,X_<sub>2</sub>_,...,X<sub>n</sub>_, each clause consisting of three literals. The goal is to decide whether \(\phi\) is satisfiable. For our reduction, we construct a MinGMConn instance \((P_\phi,D_\phi)\) and a positive integer \(\alpha=\alpha(\phi)\) such that \((P_\phi,D_\phi)\) has an optimal solution of size \(\alpha\) if and only if \(\phi\) is satisfiable (Lemmas 15 and 18). This immediately implies Theorem 1. In the following, we identify a demand \(d\in D_\phi\) with its demand rectangle _R(d_). This allows us to speak, for example, of intersections of demands, corners of demands, or points covered by demands.

Our construction of the MinGMConn instance \((P_\phi,D_\phi)\) is based on different _gadgets_ and their connections among each other. A gadget can be thought of as a rectangle in the Euclidean plane that contains a specific set of input points and demands between these. We start with a coarse overview of our construction by describing how gadgets are placed and how they interact (Figure 2). We then give the intuition behind our reduction and describe the detailed inner structure of gadgets afterward (Figure 3). Because of space constraints, the actual proof of the NP-hardness is given in Appendix D.

**Overview of the Construction.** For each clause _C<sub>j</sub>_, we create a _clause gadget GC<sub>j</sub>_ and for each variable _X<sub>i</sub>_, a _variable gadget GX<sub>i</sub>_. Clause gadgets are arranged along a descending diagonal line, so all of _GC<sub>j</sub>_ is to the bottom-right of _GC_<sub>_j_-1</sub>. Variable gadgets are arranged in<tbc>

the same manner. This avoids unwanted interference among different clause and variable gadgets, respectively. The variable gadgets are placed to the bottom-left of all clause gadgets.

For each positive occurrence of a variable _X<sub>i</sub>_ in a clause _C<sub>j</sub>_, we place a dedicated _connection point_ \(p_{ij}^+\in P_\phi\) as well as suitable _connection demands_ from \(p_{ij}^+\) to a dedicated inner point of _GX<sub>i</sub>_ and to a dedicated inner point of _GC<sub>j</sub>_. Their purpose is to force optimal MinGMConn solutions to create specific M-paths (going first up and then right in a narrow corridor) connecting a variable to the clauses in which it appears positively. We call the area covered by these two demands a _(positive) variable-clause path_. Similarly, there are connection points \(p_{ij}^-\in P_\phi\) with suitable demands for negative appearances of _X<sub>i</sub>_ in _C<sub>j</sub>_, creating a _(negative) variable-clause path_ (going first right and then up in a narrow corridor).

Finally, there is a _starting point_ \(S\in P_\phi\) to the bottom-left of all other points. It has a demand to a _clause point c<sub>j</sub>_ in the top-right of each clause gadget _GC<sub>j</sub>_ (an _SC demand_) and to a _variable point x<sub>i</sub>_ in the bottom-left of each variable gadget _GX<sub>i</sub>_ (an _SX demand_). The inside of clause gadgets simply provides different entrance points for the variable-clause paths, while the inside of variable gadgets forces an optimal solution to choose between using either only positive or only negative variable-clause paths. We will use these choices inside variable gadgets to identify an optimal solution for \((P_\phi,D_\phi)\) with a variable assignment for \(\phi\). Details about clause and variable gadgets are given in Figure 3 and at the end of this section.

The first part of the reduction (Lemma 15) shows that if \(\phi\) is satisfiable, then there is an (optimal) solution \(Q_\phi\) of size \(\alpha\). This is proven by constructing a family of _boolean solutions_. These are (partial) solutions \(Q_\phi\) that can be identified with a variable assignment for \(\phi\) and that have the following properties: \(Q_\phi\) has size \(\alpha\) and satisfies all non-_SC_ demands. Additionally, it can satisfy an _SC_ demand (_S,c<sub>j</sub>_) only by going through some variable _x<sub>i</sub>_, where such a path exists if and only if _C<sub>j</sub>_ is satisfied by the value assigned to _X<sub>i</sub>_ by (the variable assignment) \(Q_\phi\). In particular, if \(\phi\) is satisfiable, there is a boolean solution \(Q_\phi\) satisfying all _SC_ demands. This implies that \(Q_\phi\) is a solution to \((P_\phi,D_\phi)\) of (optimal) size \(\alpha\).

Lemma 18 provides the other direction of the reduction, stating that if there is a solution \(Q_\phi\) for \((P_\phi,D_\phi)\) of size \(\alpha\), then \(\phi\) is satisfiable. Its proof is more involved and is made possible by careful placement of gadgets, connection points, and demands. In a first step, we show that the small size of \(Q_\phi\) implies that different parts of our construction each must be satisfied by only a few, dedicated points from \(Q_\phi\). For example, \(Q_\phi\) has to use exactly _n_ points to satisfy the _n SX_ demands (_S,x<sub>i</sub>_). Another result (Proposition 16) about "triangular" instances (e.g., the triangular grid formed by the _n SX_ demands, see Figure 2) states that, here, optimal solutions must lie on grid lines inside the "triangle". We conclude that any M-path from _S_ to a clause point _c<sub>j</sub>_ must go through exactly one variable point _x<sub>i</sub>_. Similarly, we show that the 6_m_ connection demands (forming the 3_m_ variable-clause paths) are satisfied by 6_m_ points from \(Q_\phi\) and, since they are so few, each of these points lies in the corner of a connection demand. This ensures that M-paths cannot cheat by, e.g., "jumping" between different variable-clause paths. More precisely, such a path can be entered only at the variable gadget where it starts and be left only at the clause gadget where it ends.

All that remains to show is that there cannot be two M-paths entering a variable gadget _GX<sub>i</sub>_ (which they must do via _x<sub>i</sub>_) such that one leaves through a positive and the other through a negative variable-clause path. We can then interpret \(Q_\phi\) as a boolean solution (the variable assignment for _X<sub>i</sub>_ being determined by whether M-paths leave _GX<sub>i</sub>_ through positive or through negative variable- clause paths). Since \(Q_\phi\) satisfies all demands, in particular all _SC_ demands, the corresponding variable assignment satisfies all clauses.

**Details of Clause & Variable Gadgets.** We recommend to keep Figures 3a and 3b close at hand when reading the following gadget descriptions. The _clause gadget GC<sub>j</sub>_ for clause _C<sub>j</sub>_ contains the _clause point c<sub>j</sub>_ and three _(clause) literal points_ \(\ell_{j1},\ell_{j2},\ell_{j3}\). The clause point is in the top-right. The literal points represent the literals of _C<sub>j</sub>_ and form a descending diagonal within the gadget such that positive are above negative literals. ## 4 An Approximation Algorithm for _s_-Thin Instances

In this section, we present and analyze an aproximation algorithm for _s_-thin instances (where points in _P_ lie on at most _s_ distinct _x_-coordinates). In particular, we allow more than one point to share an _x_-coordinate. However, we still require any two distinct points to have distinct _y_-coordinates. We show an approximation ratio of _O_(log_s_), proving Theorem 2.

An _x-group_ is a maximal subset of _P_ having the same _x_-coordinate. Note that an _O_(log_s_)- approximation for _s_-thin instances can be obtained via a natural "vertical" divide-and-conquer algorithm that recursively divides the _s_ many _x_-groups in two subinstances with roughly _s/_2 many _x_- groups each. (Section E.2 contains a more general version of this algorithm subdividing into an arbitrary number of subinstances.) The analysis of this algorithm uses the number of input points as a lower bound on OPT. However, such a bound is not sufficient for our purpose of deriving an \(O(\sqrt{logn})\)-approximation.

In this section, we present a different algorithm, based on "horizontal" divide-and-conquer (after a pre-processing step to sparsify the set of _y_-coordinates in the input via minimum hitting sets). Additionally, we show that the size of a such a set is always upper bounded by the maximum number of vertically separable demands. Even more importantly, our stronger bound allow us to prove Theorem 3 in the next section since vertically separable demands fulfill the subadditivity property mentioned in the introduction. ## 5 A Sublogarithmic Approximation Algorithm

In this section, we give an overview of how to leverage the _O_(log_s_)-approximation for _s_-thin instances to design an \(O(\sqrt{logn})\)-approximation algorithm for general instances.

### Sub-instances.

Let (_P,D_) be an instance of MinGMConn and let _B_ be a bounding box for _P_, that is, \(P\subseteq B\). Let S={_S_<sub>1</sub>_,...,S<sub>s</sub>_} be a collection of _s_ vertical strips, ordered from left to right, that are obtained by drawing _s_-1 vertical lines that partition _B_. We naturally create _s_+1 sub-instances as follows. (See also Figure 4.) First, we have _s intra-strip instances_ \(\{(P_i,D_i)\}_{i\in[s]}\) such that \(P_i=P\cap S_i\) and \(D_i=D\cap(S_i\times S_i)\). Next, we have the _inter-strip instance_ \(\pi_\mathcal{S}(D)=(P',D')\) where \(P'\) is obtained by collapsing each strip in S into a single column and \(D'\) is obtained from collapsing demands accordingly. For each point \(p\in P\), denote by \(\pi_\mathcal{S}(p)\) a copy of _p_ in \(P'\) after collapsing. Note that this is a simplified description of the instances that avoids some technicalities. For a precise definition, see Appendix E.

### Sub-additivity of VS.

The following is our sub-additivity property that we use crucially in our divide-and-conquer algorithm.

**Lemma 12.** _If_ (_P,D_) _is an instance of_ MinGMConn _with strip subdivision_ S_, then_<tbc>

\(\mathsf{VS}(P,D)\ge\mathsf{VS}(\pi_\mathcal{S}(P,D))+\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}\mathsf{VS}(P\cap S,D\cap(S\times S)).\)

_Proof._ Let \((P',D')=\pi_\mathcal{S}(P,D)\) be the inter-strip instance. Let \(D''\subseteq D'\) be a vertically separable demand subset of size \(\mathsf{VS}(P',D')\). Let \(D_\mathsf{I}=\{(p,q)\in D|(\pi_\mathcal{S}(p),\pi_\mathcal{S}(q))\in D''\}\) be the demand subset of _D_ corresponding to \(D''\). For any \(S\in\mathcal{S}\), let _D_<sub>S</sub> be a vertically separable demand subset of \(D\cap(S\times S)\) of cardinality \(\mathsf{VS}(P\cap S,D\cap(S\times S))\). We claim that \(D_\mathsf{I}\cup\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal{S}}D_S\) is a vertically separable demand subset of _D_. Obviously, its size is equal to the right side of the inequality that we want to prove.

Since \(D''\) is vertically separable, we can sequentially cut it via vertical line segments. W.l.o.g. we may assume that these segments lie on strip boundaries. Observe also that any vertical line segment _z_ on some strip boundary cuts (intersects) some rectangle \(R(\pi_\mathcal{S}(p),\pi_\mathcal{S}(q))\) with \((\pi_\mathcal{S}(p),\pi_\mathcal{S}(q))\in D''\) if and only if cuts (intersects) _R(p,q_) where \((p,q)\in D_\mathsf{I}\). Hence, the same sequence of vertical line segments on the strip boundaries that cuts \(D''\) also cuts _D_<sub>I</sub>.

After cutting _D_<sub>I</sub>, process the strips \(S\in\mathcal{S}\) in an arbitrary order and cut the demand set _D<sub>S</sub>_ with segments contained in the interior of _S_. Obviously, there is no interference between cutting within different strips and none of the segments we used for cutting _D_<sub>I</sub> intersects any rectangle in _D<sub>S</sub>_ because they lie on the strip boundaries.

**Divide-and-conquer.** Choose the strips S so that \(s=|\mathcal{S}|=2^{\sqrt{logn}}\). Thus the inter-strip instance admits an approximation of ratio \(O(logs)=O(\sqrt{logn})\); in fact, we obtain a solution of cost \(O(\sqrt{logn})\mathsf{VS}(\pi_\mathcal{S}(P,D))\). We recursively solve each intra-strip instance (_P<sub>i</sub>,D<sub>i</sub>_), and combine the solutions from these _s_+1 sub-instances. (Details on how the solution can be combined are deferred to Appendix E.)

We show by induction on the number of points that for any instance (_P,D_) the cost of the computed solution is \(O(\sqrt{logn})\mathsf{VS}(P,D)\). (Here, we do not take into account the cost incurred by combining the solutions to the sub-instances.) By induction hypothesis, we have for each (_P<sub>i</sub>,D<sub>i</sub>_) a solution of cost \(O(\sqrt{logn})\mathsf{VS}(P_i,D_i)\) since |_P<sub>i</sub>|\<|P_|. Note that we cannot use the induction hypothesis for the inter-strip instance since \(|P'|=|P|\), which is why we need the _O_(log_s_)-approximation algorithm. Using sub-additivity we obtain:

\(O(\sqrt{logn})\left(\mathsf{VS}(\pi_\mathcal{S}(P,D))+\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}\mathsf{VS}(P\cap S,D\cap(S\times S))\right)=O(\sqrt{logn})\mathsf{VS}(P,D).\)

There is an additional cost incurred by combining the solutions of the sub-instances to a feasible solution of the current instance. In Appendix E we argue that this can be done at a cost of _O_(OPT) for each of the \(logn/logs=\sqrt{logn}\) many levels of the recursion. For the _nXD_ demands (_x<sub>i</sub>,d<sub>i</sub>_) however, we add _either_ the top-left corner of the demand \((x_i,x_i^+)\) _or_ of the demand \((x_i,x_i^-)\) to \(Q_\phi\). Note that in both cases, since \(x_i^+\) and \(x_i^-\) each have already established a trivial connection to _d<sub>i</sub>_, we get a M-path from _x<sub>i</sub>_ to _d<sub>i</sub>_, satisfying the _XD_ demand (_x<sub>i</sub>,d<sub>i</sub>_).

Any (partial) solution \(Q_\phi\) constructed in this way has size \(\alpha\) (it contains one new point for each non-_SC_ demand), satisfies all non-_SC_ demands, and may or may not satisfy some _SC_ demands. Moreover, there is a natural one-to-one mapping between such partial solutions and variable assignments for \(\phi\) (set _X<sub>i</sub>_=1 if and only if (_x<sub>i</sub>,d<sub>i</sub>_) is satisfied via \(x_i^+\)). Now consider which _SC_ demands are satisfied by such a solution/variable assignment \(Q_\phi\). Note that \(Q_\phi\) yields a M-path from \(x_i^+\) to _c<sub>j</sub> if and only if C<sub>j</sub>_ contains the positive literal _X<sub>i</sub>_ (the M-path can then use the corresponding positive variable-clause path). Similarly, \(Q_\phi\) produces a M-path from \(x_i^-\) to _c<sub>j</sub> if and only if C<sub>j</sub>_ contains the negative literal \(\neg X_i\). On the other hand, \(Q_\phi\) yields a M-path from _S_ to \(x_i^+\) _if and only if_ the variable assignment \(Q_\phi\) sets _X<sub>i</sub>_=1 and a M-path from _S_ to \(x_i^-\) otherwise. Together, we get a M-path from _S_ to _c<sub>j</sub>_ if and only if _C<sub>j</sub>_ is satisfied via _X<sub>i</sub>_ in the variable assignment \(Q_\phi\). As a consequence, the solution \(Q_\phi\) satisfies exactly those _SC_ demands (_S,c<sub>j</sub>_) for which _C<sub>j</sub>_ is satisfied by the variable assignment \(Q_\phi\). In summary, \(Q_\phi\) is a boolean solution (as defined in Section 3).

Now, if \(\phi\) is satisfiable, fix a solution \(Q_\phi\) that corresponds to a satisfying variable assignment. From the above it follows that \(Q_\phi\) has size \(\alpha\) and satisfies all demands in \(D_\phi\).

The remainder of this section proves the remaining direction, namely that any solution of size \(\alpha\) implies that \(\phi\) is satisfiable (Lemma 18). As this turns out to be more involved, we require some preparation. First, we provide a simple result about the structure of "triangular" instances. Afterwards, we describe a partitioning of \((P_\phi,D_\phi)\) and \(Q_\phi\) into suitable subinstances/-solutions (some of which are triangular). This allows us to argue separately about the structure of these subinstances (triangular instances and the variable-clause paths), which will help us to get the desired result.

### Triangular Instances.

A _triangular instance_ \((P_\Delta,D_\Delta)\) of size \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) consists of _n_+1 input points \(P_\Delta=\{p_0,p_1,\dots,p_n\}\) and of _n_ demands \(D_\Delta=\{(p_0,p_i)|i\in[n]\}\). The points _p_<sub>1</sub>_,p_<sub>2</sub>_,...,p<sub>n</sub>_ form a descending diagonal and lie to the top-right of _p_<sub>0</sub>. We refer to the point set \(G_\Delta:=\{(x,y)|\exists i,j\in[n]_0:x=x(p_i),y=y(p_j)\}\cap R(D_\Delta)\) as the _(triangular) grid_ of \((P_\Delta,D_\Delta)\).

Optimal solutions for triangular instances have size _n_, since there are solutions of that size (e.g., the _n_ grid points above _p_<sub>0</sub>) and the _n_ demands from \(D_\Delta\) are monotone and vertically separable (implying a lower bound of _n_ by Lemma 6). The next proposition states that any optimal solution to a triangular instance lies on the instance’s triangular grid.

**Proposition 16.** _Consider a triangular instance_ \((P_\Delta,D_\Delta)\) _of size_ \(n\in\mathbb{N}\)_. If_ \(Q_\Delta\) _has size n and satisfies_ \(D_\Delta\)_, then_ \(Q_\Delta\) _is a subset of the instance’s grid_ \(G_\Delta\).

_Proof._ The proposition holds trivially for _n_=1, since then the sole solution point must lie either in the top-left or in the bottom-right corner of the sole demand (_p_<sub>0</sub>_,p_<sub>1</sub>). For the case of a contradiction, assume the proposition is not true for all \(n\in\mathbb{N}\backslash\{1\}\) and fix the smallest _n_ for which this is the case. So there is a triangular instance \((P_\Delta,D_\Delta)\) of size _n_ as well as a corresponding solution \(Q_\Delta\) of size _n_ that contains a non-grid point \(q\in Q_\Delta\backslash G_\Delta\). Without loss of generality, assume _p_<sub>0</sub>=(0,0).

Depending on the position of _q_, transform \((P_\Delta,D_\Delta)\) into a suitable triangular instance \((P'_\Delta,D'_\Delta)\) of size _n_-1 with a corresponding solution \(Q'_\Delta\) of size at most _n_-1 containing a non-grid point. Once this is achieved, we immediately get a contradiction to the minimality of _n_.

Consider first the case \(x(q)\unknown x(p_1)\). We transform \((P_\Delta,D_\Delta)\) into \((P'_\Delta,D'_\Delta)\) by removing both the input point _p_<sub>1</sub> and the demand (_p_<sub>0</sub>_,p_<sub>1</sub>) and by projecting _p_<sub>0</sub> to the _x_-coordinate _x(p_<sub>1</sub>) (not changing its _y_-coordinate). To construct \(Q'_\Delta\) from \(Q_\Delta\) we project all points with _x_-coordinate at most _x(p_<sub>1</sub>) to _x_-coordinate _x(p_<sub>1</sub>) and remove any points with _y_-coordinate _\>y(p_<sub>2</sub>) (which cannot help to connect _p_<sub>0</sub> to any of _p_<sub>2</sub>_,p_<sub>3</sub>_,...,p<sub>n</sub>_). One can easily check that \(Q'_\Delta\) is a solution for \((P'_\Delta,D'_\Delta)\): Any M-path going through one of the projected points remains intact, as the projected point is still reachable from the projection of _p_<sub>0</sub> (by going straight up). Moreover, \(|Q'_\Delta|<|Q_\Delta|\), since we either removed the top-left grid point if it was in \(Q_\Delta\) (since it has _y_-coordinate _y(p_<sub>1</sub>)_\>y(p_<sub>2</sub>)) or at least two of the projected points had the same _y_-coordinate (or there could not be a M-path from _p_<sub>0</sub> to _p_<sub>1</sub> in \(Q_\Delta\)), causing them to get merged during the projection. Note that \(q\in Q'_\Delta\), since this case assumes \(x(q)\unknown x(p_1)\), such that _q_ is not affected by the projection. As stated above, we get a contradiction to the minimality of _n_.

The case \(y(q)\unknown y(p_n)\) yields the same contradiction via a symmetrical argument. Thus, it remains to consider the case that _q_ and all other non-grid points have _x_-coordinate _\<x(p_<sub>1</sub>) and _y_- coordinate _\<y(p<sub>n</sub>_). Then there must we some M-path that leaves either the _x_- or the _y_-axis at some non-grid point \(q_1\in Q_\Delta\) to reach another non-grid point \(q_2\in Q_\Delta\). We consider only the case that _q_<sub>1</sub> lies on the _y_-axis; the other case is proven symmetrically. We transform \((P_\Delta,D_\Delta)\) into \((P'_\Delta,D'_\Delta)\) using the same construction as above (projecting everything left of _p_<sub>1</sub> onto _x(p_<sub>1</sub>)). This causes _q_<sub>1</sub> and _q_<sub>2</sub> to merge (giving \(|Q'_\Delta|<|Q_\Delta|\)) and ensures the existence of a non-grid point in \(Q'_\Delta\) (the projection of _q_<sub>1</sub> and _q_<sub>2</sub>). Again, as stated above, this yields a contradiction to the minimality of _n_.

**Partitioning the Instance & Solution.** Consider a solution \(Q_\phi\) to \((P_\phi,D_\phi)\) with \(|Q_\phi|=\alpha\). We partition \((P_\phi,D_\phi)\) and \(Q_\phi\) into suitable subinstances \((P_\bullet,D_\bullet)\) and subsolutions \(Q_\bullet\) such that the different \((P_\bullet,D_\bullet)\) cover different areas, \(Q_\bullet\) solves \((P_\bullet,D_\bullet)\), and \(|Q_\bullet|=|D_\bullet|\). This will allow us to argue about the structure of these different subsolutions in the proof of Lemma 18 (e.g., by realizing that one of the subinstances is a triangular solution, such that we can apply Proposition 16). For our partitioning, define

- \(D_{SC}=\{(S,c_j)|j\in[m]\}\) (the _m SC_ demands),<tbc>

- \(D_{SX}=\{(S,x_i)|i\in[n]\}\) (the _n SX_ demands),<tbc>

- \(D_{cl}=\{(\ell_{jk},c_j)|j\in[m],k\in[3]\}\) (the 3_m_ demands in clause gadgets),<tbc>

**-** \(D_{var}=\{d\in D_\phi|\exists i\in[n]:\{x_i^+,x_i^-,d_i\}\cap d\neq\emptyset\}\) (the 3_m_+3_n_ demands in variable gadgets).

With this, we have \(D_\overline{SC}=D\backslash D_{SC}=D_{SX}\cup D_{cl}\cup D_{con}\cup D_{var}\). Thus, we get a natural partition \(Q_\phi=Q_{SX}\cup Q_{cl}\cup Q_{var}\cup Q_{con}\), with \(Q_\bullet=\{q\in Q_\phi|q\in R(D_\bullet)\}\), such that \(Q_\bullet\) satisfies \(D_\bullet\). We will use this to show that \(Q_\phi\) cannot "cheat" by jumping between different variable-clause paths, but instead must enter a variable-clause path at its entrance (at some variable gadget) and leave it at its exit (at some clause gadget).

**Proposition 17.** _Q<sub>con</sub> satisfies each demand_ \(d\in D_{con}\) _via a dedicated point_ \(q_d\in Q_{con}\) _that lies in the top-left or bottom-right corner of d._

We call a connection demand \(d\in D_{con}\) either _horizontal_ or _vertical_, depending on whether _d_ leaves a variable/clause gadget horizontally or vertically. Our construction ensures that no point is covered by more than two connection demands and that both the top-left and bottom-right corner of a connection demand are not contained in any other connection demand. Moreover, if two connection demands intersect, one is horizontal and one is vertical.

Assume the statement is not true, so there is a \(d\in D_{con}\) for which neither its top-left nor its bottom-right corner is in _Q<sub>con</sub>_. We consider only the case that _d_ is a horizontal connection demand; the vertical case is symmetrical. Then there must be two points \(q_1,q_2\in Q_{con}\cap R(d)\) that share the same _x_-coordinate. Both of them must be covered by a vertical connection demand \(d'\), since otherwise we found two points in _Q<sub>con</sub>_ covered by only one demand from _D<sub>con</sub>_, a contradiction to Corollary 7. If _Q<sub>con</sub>_ contains the top-left or bottom-right corner of \(R(d')\) (which cannot be covered by any other connection demand), we found three points in _Q<sub>con</sub>_ (_q_<sub>1</sub>_,q_<sub>2</sub>, and the corner) covered by only two demands from _D<sub>con</sub>_ (_d_ and \(d'\)), which is again a contradiction to Corollary 7. Thus, _Q<sub>con</sub>_ cannot contain a corner of \(R(d')\), which implies two points \(q'_1,q'_2\in Q_{con}\cap R(d')\) that share the same _y_-coordinate. If \(\{q_1,q_2\}\cap\{q'_1,q'_2\}\neq\emptyset\), this intersection has size exactly three. But then we found three points in \(R(d)\cap R(d')\), an area that cannot be intersected by a third connection demand, yielding again a contradiction to Corollary 7. So we must have \(\{q_1,q_2\}\cap\{q'_1,q'_2\}=\emptyset\). This yields the final contradiction to Corollary 7, since we found four points in _Q<sub>con</sub>_ covered by at most three connection demands from _D<sub>con</sub>_ (_d_, \(d'\), and a potential third horizontal connection demand covering \(q'_1\) and \(q'_2\)).

With this, we are ready to prove the second direction of the reduction:

**Lemma 18.** _If there is a solution to_ \((P_\phi,D_\phi)\) _of size_ \(\alpha\)_, then_ \(\phi\) _is satisfiable._

_Proof._ Consider a solution \(Q_\phi\) to \((P_\phi,D_\phi)\) with \(|Q_\phi|=\alpha\). We basically show that \(Q_\phi\) is a boolean solution, such that it corresponds to a satisfying variable assignment for \(\phi\) (since it satisfies all _SC_ demands). To this end, remember the partitioning of \((P_\phi,D_\phi)\) and \(Q_\phi\) described above. As detailed above, each \((P_\bullet,D_\bullet)\) with solution \(Q_\bullet\) satisfies the preconditions of Corollary 7. We use this to argue about the structure of the different \(Q_\bullet\).

We start with the structure of _Q<sub>SX</sub>_. Observe that (_P<sub>SX</sub>,D<sub>SX</sub>_) is a triangular instance of size _n_ that is satisfied by the solution _Q<sub>SX</sub>_ of size _n_. By Proposition 16, _Q<sub>SX</sub>_ lies on the triangular grid<tbc>

<tbc>of (_P<sub>SX</sub>,D<sub>SX</sub>_). As an immediate consequence, any M-path that satisfies an _SC_ demand (_S,c<sub>j</sub>_) must go through one of the variable points _x<sub>i</sub>_ (note that no \(q\in Q_\phi\backslash Q_{SX}\) can share an _x_- or _y_-coordinate with _S_, since none of the demands \(d\in D_\overline{SC}\backslash D_{SX}\) would cover such a _q_).

Next, remember that Proposition 17 restricts _Q<sub>con</sub>_ to the corners of _D<sub>con</sub>_. This implies that a M-path entering _GX<sub>i</sub>_ through _x<sub>i</sub>_ cannot immediately leave _GX<sub>i</sub>_ but must first go through the inside of _GX<sub>i</sub>_. Otherwise, there would be some \(q\in Q_\phi\) outside of _GX<sub>i</sub>_ either with _x(q_)=_x(x<sub>i</sub>_) and _y(q)\>y(x<sub>i</sub>_) or with _y(q_)=_y(x<sub>i</sub>_) and _x(q)\>x(x<sub>i</sub>_). This _q_ must be covered by some demand \(d\in D_\overline{SC}\), and our construction is such that this can only be done for a \(d\in D_{con}\) (see Figure 2). That is \(q\in Q_{con}\), and Proposition 17 then implies that _q_ lies in the corner of _d_. But no corner of a connection demand shares an _x_- or _y_-coordinate with _x<sub>i</sub>_ (see Figure 2), such that _q_ cannot exist.

A simple consequence of this is that any M-path entering variable _GX<sub>i</sub>_ (through _x<sub>i</sub>_) can leave _GX<sub>i</sub>_ only by entering one of the connection demands \((x_{ik}^+,p_{ij}^+)\) or \((x_{ik}^-,p_{ij}^-)\) (see Figure 3b) and must then follow the corresponding variable-clause path to _GC<sub>j</sub>_ (see Figure 2).

So in summary, any M-path from _S_ to a clause point _c<sub>j</sub>_ must enter some variable gadget _GX<sub>i</sub>_ at _x<sub>i</sub>_, which it then must leave either through a positive or negative variable-clause path to reach a connected clause gadget _GC<sub>j</sub>_. Note that _Q<sub>cl</sub>_ guarantees that this M-path actually reaches _c<sub>j</sub>_ (in fact, Proposition 16 implies a strict structure on _Q<sub>cl</sub>_, but we do not need this for our proof). In the next and final step, we argue about the structure of _Q<sub>var</sub>_, showing that _x<sub>i</sub>_ cannot be connected to both a positive and negative variable-clause path. Once this is shown, we can identify \(Q_\phi\) with the variable assignment that assigns _X<sub>i</sub>_=1 if and only if _x<sub>i</sub>_ is connected to positive variable-clause paths and _X<sub>i</sub>_=0 otherwise. So consider _Q<sub>var</sub>_. For any \(i\in[n]\) there must be a dedicated \(q_i\in Q_{var}\) on the left or bottom side of the _XD_ demand \((x_i,d_i)\in D_{var}\). ## E Sublogarithmic Approximation for MinGMConn

In this section, we present the algorithm underlying Theorem 3, that is, an algorithm with approximation ratio \(O(\sqrt{logn})\). The idea is to divide the plane into \(s\checkmark n\) many vertical strips, where _s_ can be thought of as a function that is sublinear in n. We call demands between points lying within the same strip _intra-strip demands_ and between points in different strips _inter-strip demands_. In order to satisfy the intra-strip demands, we recursively execute the algorithm (with fixed recursion parameter _s_) and exploit that demand pairs in different strips are independent. To satisfy the inter-strip demands, we project points to the adjacent strip boundaries. This results in an instance with \(s\checkmark n\) many distinct _x_ coordinates for which we can apply the algorithm HorizontalManhattan presented in the previous section.

### E.1 Algorithm Description

Before giving an overview of Algorithm 3, we discuss its building blocks and some notation.

### Input.

The input consists of an instance (_P,D_) of MinGMConn and a parameter _s_ specifying the number of sub-problems (strips) in which the algorithm should divide the instance. As in the previous section, we allow that distinct points in _P_ have the same _x_-coordinate but require distinct _y_- coordinates. Again, we may assume monotone demands.

### Subdivision into Strips.

Let (_P,D_) be an instance of MinGMConn. Let \(s\ge 2\) be a positive integer and let _B_ be a set of _s_-1 distinct vertical lines in the plane. The lines in _B_ partition the plane into a set S of _s_ many vertical strips. We call the lines in _B strip boundaries_ of S, where each strip has one or two strip boundaries (left and right). We call S a _strip subdivision of_ (_P,D_) if each boundary of S is disjoint from _P_.

Let _g_ be the number of _x_-groups in _P_. In line 2, we compute a strip division S such that each strip contains at most \(\lceil g/s\rceil\) many _x_-groups. We call such a strip subdivision _balanced_.

### Intra-Strip Instances.

We first satisfy intra-strip demand pairs (Algorithm 3, Line 4). To this end, we invoke the algorithm recursively for each strip _S_ and solve the sub-instance of (_P,D_), which satisfies all demands in _D_ lying completely in _S_ (intra-strip instance). The result is added to our solution _Q_.

### Inter-Strip Instances.

Consider an instance (_P,D_) of MinGMConn and a strip subdivision S with strips _S_<sub>1</sub>_,...,S<sub>s</sub>_ ordered left-to-right. For each input point \(p\in P\), there is a unique strip \(S\in\mathcal{S}\) containing _p_. If \(S\neq S_1\), then we denote by \(\pi_\mathcal{S}^1(p)\) the horizontal projection of _p_ to the left boundary of _S_. Analogously, if \(S\neq S_s\), then we denote by \(\pi_\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{r}(p)\) the horizontal projection of _p_ to the right boundary of _S_. For any subset \(P'\subseteq P\), we define \(\pi_\mathcal{S}^1(P')=\{\pi_\mathcal{S}^1(p)|p\in P'\backslash S_1\}\), \(\pi_\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{r}(P')=\{\pi_\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{r}(p)|p\in P'\backslash S_s\}\), and \(\pi_\mathcal{S}(P')=\pi_\mathcal{S}^1(P')\cup\pi_\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{r}(P')\) as the set of horizontal projections of the points in \(P'\) to left, right, and both strip boundaries of their respective strips in S, respectively.

Define a new instance on the projection \(\pi_\mathcal{S}(P)\) of _P_ to the adjacent strip boundaries by

\(\pi_\mathcal{S}(D)=\{(\pi_\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{r}(p),\pi_\mathcal{S}^1(q))|(p,q)\in D\text{and}p,q\text{lie in different and non-adjacent strips}\},\)

the "projected" demands. (Recall that we assumed that _x(p)\<x(q)._) We drop demands within the same strip as they are handled in the respective intra-strip instance and demands from adjacent strips because are projected to the same boundary and thus automatically satisfied. Call \(\pi_\mathcal{S}(P,D):=(\pi_\mathcal{S}(P),\pi_\mathcal{S}(D))\) the _inter-strip instance_ corresponding to (_P,D_). Note that the input points of this resulting instance share _s_-1 many distinct _x_-coordinates.

Intuitively, the following lemma states that a feasible solution to the inter-strip distance along with the projected points satisfies all the demand-pairs for which not both points are in the same strip. This fact is used in algorithm and analysis.

**Lemma 19.** _Let_ (_P,D_) _be an instance with strip subdivision_ S_. If Q is a feasible solution to the inter-strip instance_ \(\pi_\mathcal{S}(P,D)\)_, then_ \(Q\cup\pi_\mathcal{S}(P)\) _satisfies all demands_ \((p,q)\in D\) _for which p and q lie in different strips._

_Proof._ To see the feasibility of \(Q\cup\pi_\mathcal{S}(P)\) consider a demand \((p,q)\in D\) where _p_ and _q_ lie in different strips. Observe that we can connect _p_ to \(\pi_\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{r}(p)\) directly, then \(\pi_\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{r}(p)\) to \(\pi_\mathcal{S}^1(q)\) via _Q_, and finally connect \(\pi_\mathcal{S}^1(q)\) to _q_ to obtain a Manhattan path from _p_ to _q_. Recall that \(\pi_\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{r}(p)\) and \(\pi_\mathcal{S}^1(q)\) are automatically connected if _p_ and _q_ lie in adjacent strips.

By Lemma 11 and Corollary 20, we can bound the total cost of points added to our solution in line 6 for solving the inter-strip instances by \(\sum_{(P^\prime,D^\prime)\in\mathcal{M}}O(log(s))\cdot\mathsf{VS}(P',D')\le O(log(s))\cdot\mathsf{VS}(P,D)\le O(log(s))\cdot\mathsf{OPT}(P,D).\) To bound the cost of points added in Line 7 via projection, note that there are _O_(log_n/_log_s_) levels of recursion. Since each point ends up in precisely one sub-instance upon the recursive calls in Line 4 each original input point contributes at most two points to the projection computed in Line 7 at each recursion level. Hence, the overall cost of this step is \(O(logn/logs)\cdot|P|=O(logn/logs)\cdot\mathsf{OPT}(P,D)\). Adding these two cost components gives an overall cost of \(O(logs+logn/logs)\cdot\mathsf{OPT}(P,D)\). The theorem follows by setting \(s=2^{\sqrt{logn}}\). **Algorithm 3:** VerticalManhattan(_P,D,s_)

## F Towards Better Approximation

In this section, we state some structural properties and show that these would imply a better approximation ratio of _O_(loglog_n_). Furthermore, we prove that those properties hold for a special class of demands.

### F.1 Structural Properties for _O_(loglog_n_)-approximation

Let _f_ be a lower bound function on OPT, that is \(f(P,D)\le O(\mathsf{OPT}(P,D))\) for any input (_P,D_). We say that _f_ satisfies _subadditivity_ if for any strip partitioning S, we have

\(f(\pi_\mathcal{S}(P,D))+\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}f(P\cap S,D\cap(S\times S))\le f(P,D).\)

For any lower bound function _f_, an _f-sparsification algorithm_ is an efficient algorithm that, on input (_P,D_), produces an instance \((\tilde{P},\tilde{D})\) such that (i) any feasible solution _Q_ for \((\tilde{P},\tilde{D})\) is feasible for (_P,D_) as well, and (ii) \(|\tilde{P}|=O(f(\tilde{P},\tilde{D}))\). The following theorem is given implicitly in \[1\]. The proof is a verbatim adaptation of the original proof and therefore omitted.

**Theorem 21.** _Let f be a lower bound function. Assume that f is subadditive and that there exists an f-sparsification algorithm. Then there exists an efficient algorithm for_ MinGMConn _producing a solution of cost at most_ \(O(\mathrm{loglog}n)f(P,D)\le O(\mathrm{loglog}n)\mathsf{OPT}(P,D)\).

We do not know how to prove the existence of sparsification algorithms for general instances and leave this as an interesting open problem. However, we will show that such an algorithm exists when the demand graph is a complete _k_-partite graph.

The existence of a sparsification algorithm can be seen as a stronger property than the previously considered existence of an _O_(log_s_)-approximation algorithm when input points have at most _s_ distinct _x_-coordinates.

**Lemma 22.** _If there exists an f-sparsification algorithm for an instance_ (_P,D_) _with at most s distinct x-coordinates, then there exists an algorithm that returns a solution with cost at most O_(log_s)f(P,D)._

_Proof._ The algorithm is as follows. First, apply the _f_-sparsification algorithm on (_P,D_) to obtain \((P',D')\). Specifically, we have that \(|P'|\le O(f(P,D))\). We say that an _x_-coordinate is active if there is an input point on it. Draw a vertical partitioning line \(\ell\) in the middle such that there are \(\lceil s/2\rceil\) active _x_-coordinates to the left of \(\ell\) and the rest to the right. Let S consist of the two strips _S<sub>L</sub>,S<sub>R</sub>_ resulting from drawing the line \(\ell\). That is the strips _S<sub>L</sub>_ and _S<sub>R</sub>_ are the regions on the left and right of line \(\ell\) respectively. For each point \(p\in P'\), we add a point \(p'\) to the solution that lies on \(\ell\) and is horizontally aligned with _p_. Notice that this satisfies all demands crossing \(\ell\). Next, we recurse inside \((P'\cap S_L,D'\cap(S_L\times S_L))\) and \((P'\cap S_R,D'\cap(S_R\times S_R))\). It is easy to see that this algorithm produces a feasible solution.

To analyze the cost, notice that there are _O_(log_s_) levels of recursions. The input instance is called _level_-0 _instance_ and creates 2 sub-instances (called _level_-1 _instances_) and so on until the last level instances. There are at most 2_<sup>j</sup>_ level-_j_ instances. Let I_<sub>j</sub>_ be the collection of all level- _j_ instances. Note that the instances in I_<sub>j</sub>_ lie on 2_<sup>j</sup>_ different strips which are pairwise disjoint. Additionally, each \((\hat{P},\hat{D})\in\mathcal{I}_j\) creates \(O(f(\hat{P},\hat{D}))\) points before making recursive calls, so the total cost of level-_j_ recursions is \(O(\sum_{(\hat{P},\hat{D})\in\mathcal{I}_j}f(\hat{P},\hat{D}))\). Since these instances \((\hat{P},\hat{D})\in\mathcal{I}_j\) lie on disjoint strips, we have that \(O(\sum_{(\hat{P},\hat{D})\in\mathcal{I}_j}f(\hat{P},\hat{D}))\le O(f(P,D))\).

The algorithm we use to obtain an \(O(\sqrt{logn})\)-approximation in Section 5 can be stated in its generality as follows.

**Theorem 23.** _Let f be a lower bound function. Assume that f is subadditive and that there exists an algorithm for_ MinGMConn _that costs at most O_(log_s)f(P,D_) _for any s-thin instance_ (_P,D). Then, there exists an efficient_ \(O(\sqrt{logn})\) _approximation algorithm for_ MinGMConn.

## F.2 Complete k-partite Demands

In this section, we consider the special case of instances (_P,D_) where the demands _D_ form a complete k-partite graph. This means, we can partition _P_ into disjoint subsets _S_<sub>1</sub>_,S_<sub>2</sub>_,...,S<sub>k</sub>_ such that \(D=S_i\times S_j\) for \(i,j\in\{1,\dots,k\}\) and \(i\neq j\). Again, we allow that points share _x_-coordinates but we assume that all points have distinct _y_-coordinates.

**Lemma 24.** _Let_ (_P,D_) _be an instance with complete k-partite demands and k-partition_ \(S_1\dot{\cup}S_2\dot{\cup},\dots,\dot{\cup}S_k\)_. Then there exists an efficient algorithm that computes a complete k-partite instance_ \((\tilde{P},\tilde{D})\) _such that_

1. \(\tilde{P}\subseteq P\) _and_ \(\tilde{D}\) _is the complete k-partite demand set on k-partition_ \(S_1\cap\tilde{P},S_2\cap\tilde{P},\dots,S_k\cap\tilde{P}\)<tbc>

2. _any feasible solution Q to_ \((\tilde{P},\tilde{D})\) _is feasible for_ (_P,D_) _as well, and_<tbc>

_3._ \(|\tilde{P}|=O(\mathsf{IS}(\tilde{P},\tilde{D}))\).

_Proof._ An _essential demand_ is a pair \((s_i,s_j)\in\tilde{D}\) where \(s_i\in S_i\) and \(s_j\in S_j\) with \(x(s_i)\neq x(s_j)\), such that the vertical side of the rectangle _R(s<sub>i</sub>,s<sub>j</sub>_) containing _s<sub>i</sub>_ does not contain any other point from _P_\\_S<sub>j</sub>_, and such that the vertical side of _R(s<sub>i</sub>,s<sub>j</sub>_) containing _s<sub>j</sub>_ does not contain any other point from _P_\\_S<sub>i</sub>_.

A point is called essential if there exists some essential demand pair involving this point. A point that is not essential is called _redundant_. Removing a redundant point from the instance is safe in the sense that any feasible solution _Q_ to the reduced instance is also feasible to the original solution. To see this, let \(s_i\in S_i\) be a redundant point and let _Q_ be a feasible solution to the reduced instance with point set _P_\\{_s<sub>i</sub>_}. Let \(s_j\in S_j\) and assume w.l.o.g. that _x(s<sub>i</sub>)\<x(s<sub>j</sub>_) and _y(s<sub>i</sub>)\<y(s<sub>j</sub>_). Since _s<sub>i</sub>_ is redundant there exists a point \(s\neq s_i,s\in P\backslash S_j\) on \(\lambda(s_i,s_j)\) or a point \(s'\neq s_j,s'\in P\backslash S_i\) on \(\rho(s_i,s_j)\). Consider first the case that there exists a point \(s\neq s_i,s\in P\backslash S_j\) on \(\lambda(s_i,s_j)\). Since _Q_ is feasible for _P_\\{_s<sub>i</sub>_} there exists a Manhattan path in \((P\backslash\{s_i\})\cup Q\) from _s_ to _s<sub>j</sub>_. This path can be extended to a Manhattan path from _s<sub>i</sub>_ to _s<sub>j</sub>_ in \(P\cup Q\) by adding _s<sub>i</sub>_ as a prefix. This establishes feasibility of _Q_ for _P_. Now consider the second case that there exists a point \(s'\neq s_j,s'\in P\backslash S_i\) on \(\rho(s_i,s_j)\) but no point \(s\neq s_i,s\in P\backslash S_j\) on \(\lambda(s_i,s_j)\). Let \(s''\in P\backslash S_i\) be the lowest point on \(\rho(s_i,s_j)\). Then \((s_i,s'')\) is an essential demand contradicting the assumption that _s<sub>i</sub>_ was redundant.

Our algorithm iteratively removes redundant points until we arrive at a subset \(\tilde{P}\subseteq P\) in which every point is essential. Thus for each point \(p\in\tilde{P}\) there exists an essential demand pair. Assign the vertical side of the corresponding demand rectangle that contains _p_ as _witness_ to _p_.

The intersection graph of the witnesses is an interval graph. We claim that it has clique size at most 4. Assume to the contrary that there exists some point _q_ (not necessarily a demand point) that is contained in 5 witnesses (each of which has an associated demand point). W.l.o.g. assume that at least 3 of the associated demand points lie below _q_. Then there exists a witness (with corresponding demand point _s<sub>i</sub>_ and demand pair (_s<sub>i</sub>,s<sub>j</sub>_)) that contains two points (possibly including _s<sub>i</sub>_) such that they belong to a different partition than \(s_j\in S_j\). This contradicts the fact that the demand pair (_s<sub>i</sub>,s<sub>j</sub>_) corresponding to this witness is essential. This implies that there exists an independent set of witnesses of size at least \(|\tilde{P}|/4\) and thus a boundary independent set of size at least \(|\tilde{P}|/8\).

Combining this lemma with Theorem 21 gives the following result.

**Corollary 25.** _There is an O_(loglog_n)-approximation algorithm for_ MinGMConn _with complete k-partite demands._

## G Geometric Demands

In this section, we consider restricted demands that are defined implicitly by geometry. We present improved approximation algorithms for these instances. First, we start with some definition.

**Definition 26.** Let (_P,D_) be an input to MinGMConn. The input demand _D_ is _uniform_ in _P_ if, for every pair \(p,q\in P\), we have a demand \((p,q)\in D\).

The following theorem was proved in Harmon’s thesis \[16\].

**Theorem 27.** _There is a Greedy algorithm that, on input_ (_P,D_) _with uniform demand, produces a feasible solution of cost at most_ \(2\cdot\mathsf{OPT}(P,D)\).

**Definition 28.** Let (_P,D_) be an input to MinGMConn. The input demand _D_ is called _disk demand_ if, for each point \(p\in P\), there exists a radius _r<sub>p</sub>_ such that, \((p,q)\in D\) if and only if \(||p-q||_1\le r_p+r_q\).

In other words, the disk demands are the demands that are defined by an intersection graph of disks. A special case that is of interest to us is the following:

**Definition 29.** We say that the input demand _D_ is a _unit-disk demand_, if there exists a real number _r_ such that \((p,q)\in D\) if and only if \(|p-q|_1\le r\).

We will use the following lemma in our algorithms to bound the cost.

**Lemma 30.** _For any input such that the demand graph_ (_P,D_) _is connected,_ \(\mathsf{OPT}(P,D)\ge|P|-1\).

_Proof._ Let _X_ be the set of points added by an optimal solution. Notice that the Manhattan graph _G<sub>P</sub>_ has |_P_| singleton components. However, the Manhattan graph \(G_{X\cup P}\) contains a single component. Removing one point from any Manhattan graph can only break one component into at most two smaller components; more formally, for any point set \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(p\in Y\) , we have that the number of components in _G_<sub>_Y-p_</sub> and that in _G<sub>Y</sub>_ differs by at most one. Therefore, we must have that \(|X|\ge|P|-1\).

### G.1 Algorithms for Unit-Disk Demand

Here we present an _O_(1)-approximation algorithm. We assume without loss of generality that _D_ is connected; if not, we could apply the same arguments to each connected component separately.

The algorithm has two steps. First, we draw an arbitrary grid G where the space between consecutive horizontal and vertical grid lines is exactly _r/_2; so each grid-cell is an (_r/_2)-by-(_r/_2) cell. Assume that no input points lie on any cell boundaries. Let C be a set of grid cells _C_ such that _C_ contains some input point, that is, \(C\cap P\neq\emptyset\). For each grid cell \(C\in\mathcal{C}\), define the points \(P_C=P\cap C\) inside the cell and _D<sub>C</sub>_ be the induced demands on the points _P<sub>C</sub>_. Observe that for any two points _p,q_ in the same cell _C_, we have \(||p-q||_1\le r\), so a demand \((p,q)\in D_C\). This means that (_P<sub>C</sub>,D<sub>C</sub>_) is in fact an instance with uniform demand. We make the following simple observations.

_Observation 2._ \(\mathsf{OPT}(P,D)\ge\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}}\mathsf{OPT}(P_C,D_C)\).

Next, we define our solution points which consist of the _inner points S_<sub>1</sub> connecting the demands _D<sub>C</sub>_ in the same cell _C_, and the _outer points S_<sub>2</sub> connecting the demands \((p,p')\in D\), \(p\in C\) and \(p'\in C'\) where _C_ and \(C'\) are two different grid cells. The inner points _S_<sub>1</sub> are defined as follows. For each cell \(C\in\mathcal{C}\), we take the solution _S_<sub>1</sub>(_C_) that results from Theorem 27, and then \(S_1=\bigcup_{C\in\mathcal{C}}S_1(C)\). The outer points _S_<sub>2</sub> is also a union of _S_<sub>2</sub>(_C_). For each grid cell \(C\in\mathcal{C}\), for each point \(p\in C\) that has some demand with some other point in different cell, if a vertical grid line _L_ (a line drawn at the _x_-coordinate _x(L_)) is within distance _r_ from _p_, we create a point (_x(L),y(p_)) on line _L_ (in other words, this is a projection of point _p_ onto line _L_.) We do the same for each point \(p\in P_C\) and each horizontal grid line _L_: If _L_ is within distance _r_ from _p_, create a projected point (_x(p),y(L_)). The set _S_<sub>2</sub>(_C_) contains, for each \(p\in P_C\), all such projected points from _p_.

**Lemma 31** (Feasibility)**.** _The solution_ \(S_1\cup S_2\) _is feasible for_ (_P,D)._

_Proof._ Consider any point \((p,q)\in D\). If _p_ and _q_ are in the same cell, we are done since _S_<sub>1</sub> would connect them. If \(p\in C\) and \(q\in C'\) for \(C,C'\in\mathcal{C}\), then consider any grid line _L_ that separates them, so we have that the distance between _L_ and _p_ is at most _r_ and so is the distance between _L_ and _q_. Let \(p'\) and \(q'\) be projections of _p_ and _q_ on _L_. We have a Manhattan path \(p\rightarrow p'\rightarrow q'\rightarrow q\).

**Lemma 32** (Cost)**.** \(|S_1|+|S_2|\le O(\mathsf{OPT}(P,D))\)

_Proof._ From Theorem 27, we have that \(|S_1|\le 2\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}}\mathsf{OPT}(P_C,D_C)\le 2\mathsf{OPT}(P,D)\). Next, for points in _S_<sub>2</sub>, notice that each point \(p\in P\) creates at most 8 projected points, so we have:

\(|S_2|=\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}}|S_2(C)|\le 8\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}}|P_C|\le 8|P|\le 8\mathsf{OPT}(P,D)+8\)

The last inequality follows from Lemma 30.

## G.2 General Disks

Now we show that any instance with disc demand admits an \(O(log\Delta)\)-approximation where each \(r_p\in[1,\Delta]\). As in the proof of the unit disk case, we may assume that _G_ is connected and every input-point in _P_ is part of some demand.

Let _h,k_ be minimal and maximal integers respectively such that \(2^h\le r_p\le 2^{k-1}\) for all \(p\in P\). Fix grids \(\Gamma_h\subseteq\Gamma_{h+1}\subseteq\dots\subseteq\Gamma_k\) of sizes 2<sup>_h_-1</sup>,2_<sup>h</sup>,...,_2<sup>_k_-1</sup> respectively. For every input point, we place 8 points by projecting a point to the two closest grid lines in each direction. We do this for each of the grids adding in total \(8n(k-h+1)=O(nlog\Delta)\) many points.

Additionally, we satisfy the demands within a cell of \(\Gamma_h\) as before by applying the greedy algorithm for each cell separately, using at most \(2\cdot\mathsf{OPT}\) points. The statement follows, as \(\mathsf{OPT}\ge\frac{n}{2}\) by Lemma 30.

## G.3 Demands with Two Radii

In this section, we study the disk demands where there are only two different radii _r<sub>A</sub>\<r<sub>B</sub>_.

**Definition 33.** Let (_P,D_) be an input to MinGMConn. The input demand _D_ is called _two-disk demand_ if the point set _P_ is partitioned into two subsets \(A\cup B\), such that every point \(p\in A\) has _r<sub>p</sub>=r<sub>A</sub>_; otherwise, _r<sub>p</sub>=r<sub>B</sub>_ for each \(p\in B\).

Another demand we are interested in is the following:

**Definition 34.** Let (_P,D_) be an input to MinGMConn. The input demand _D_ is called _complete bipartite demand_ if _P_ is partitioned into two subsets \(A\cup B\) such that \((p,q)\in D\) if and only if \(p\in A\) and \(q\in B\).

**Lemma 35.** _If there is an_ \(\alpha\)_-approximation for the complete bipartite case, then there is an_ \(O(\alpha)\)_- approximation for two-disk demands. This implies an O_(loglog_n)-approximation for two-disk demand._

_Proof._ Let (_P,D_) be an input such that _D_ is a two-disk demand without isolated vertices, i.e., every point in _P_ is part of at least one demand. Define \(D_A=D\cap(A\times A)\) and \(D_B=D\cap(B\times B)\). Using the algorithm for unit-disk demands, we have an algorithm satisfying _D<sub>A</sub>_ and _D<sub>B</sub>_ using at most _O_(OPT(_A,D<sub>A</sub>_)) and _O_(OPT(_B,D<sub>B</sub>_)) points respectively, which is together _O_(OPT(_P,D_)).

Consider the grid G of size _r<sub>B</sub>/_2 used to satisfy _D<sub>B</sub>_. For each point _p_ in _A_ consider the cell \(C\in\mathcal{C}\) that contains that point. As before, \((p,q)\in D\) only for those points \(q\in C'\) such that _C_ and \(C'\) are in close proximity (that is, constant grid cells away from each other.) By projecting _p_ in each direction to the two closest grid lines, we use _O_(OPT(_P,D_)) points and satisfy all demand pairs between _A_ and _B_ for which both points lie in different grid cells. Within a cell, the remaining demands are complete bipartite. Hence, if we have an \(O(\alpha)\)-approximation for the complete bipartite case we will have a \(O(\alpha)\)-approximation for this case.
